#88042. Why aren’t mortgage rates lower after massive stock sell-off?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (644 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Why aren’t mortgage rates lower after massive stock sell-off?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%.
  • The Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through.
  • Industry observers note that I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%. So what gives?

The Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through. Now AI stocks are being slammed, with moratoriums on data centers coming in the near future as the anti-AI backlash grows. In this environment, you could expect the 10-year yield and rates to fall, but that’s not what’s happening.

Industry observers note that I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts. Let’s go over each part of this storyline.

In a recent development, oil prices were very volatile earlier this year and bond yields started moving in synch with them — especially after the first MOU deal broke off. Now that oil prices have fallen, you might expect at least a few Federal Reserve members to say that this could be a positive, but they haven’t.

In fact, when oil was trading between $68-$82, no Fed members noted anything positive, and Cleveland Fed President (and Fed hawk) Beth Hammack talked about how lower oil prices were were actually bad for inflation because people could then spend more money.

Industry observers note that in any case, so far, lower oil prices haven’t helped the 10-year yield get below 4.70%. If oil can trade between $67-$82, that would help a lot, but the last time that happened was when we unveiled a deal with Iran in June.

It has been revealed that I have used the CoreWeave stock price as an example of the problems with the AI companies. Since CoreWeave had some financing problems, the markets have soured on AI, and as you can see in the chart below, the organization’s stock price has been crushed. This has helped keep the 10-year yield below 5.35% for sure and has assisted in lower yields this week. But we are still elevated versus what we saw after the MOU deal was confirmed.

The Fed has made AI a huge inflation talking point, and they need to see much more pain in the AI sector before changing their tune.

If we were getting all this news about AI and oil prices four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield and mortgage rates would be lower today. But all this stock drama and falling oil prices came in a 14-day period where the Fed hawks came out every day talking about more Fed rate hikes, even a 50-basis-point hike. I mean, look at how the U.S. dollar hasn’t been fazed by the market drama.

Recent findings suggest that for the past two months, I have focused on two key levels for the 10-year yield: 5.35% and 5.15%. Both those levels held and yields have fallen from these points. So what lower oil prices and falling stocks have done is made sure bond yields don’t go much higher and for now, let’s take that as a victory. However, I do understand why people might be scratching their heads on why rates aren’t lower with lower oil prices and falling AI stocks.

The Fed hawks are the main reason bond yields aren’t lower; they want to make sure that the bond market doesn’t get relaxed, even with lower oil prices and falling stocks, and they have done their job well. They really want to take back all the insurance interest rate cuts from last year and because of this, the 10-year yield is still at 4.95%. If the Fed members weren’t so hawkish over the last two weeks, bond yields would be lower and we would have already had sub-7% mortgage rates.

Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, prepares Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.
  • Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, declared a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion.
  • Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, declared a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the manufacturer prepares to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, remarked Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

Industry observers note that “This is a really crucial blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he mentioned. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky stated. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Sources indicate that batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky stated Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The manufacturer must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

Recent findings suggest that the startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

It has been revealed that the tech giant has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round confirmed in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

It has been revealed that seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Recent findings suggest that group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced intends for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he stated.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

Industry observers note that “None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

Bank of America has disclosed a position in an XRP exchange-traded fund in its latest quarterly 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing, dated Nov. 16, shows that the bank held 13,260 shares of the futures-based Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI), worth about $106,600, at the end of the third quarter.

Bank of America held 13,000 shares of the fund in the first quarter and 13,260 shares in the second quarter, according to its earlier 13F filings. The same filing lists more than $685 million in BlackRock's IBIT, $13.58 million in Bitwise and $950,000 in VanEck.

It has been revealed that seven major banks disclosed XRP fund holdings worth a total of $29.4 million in filings published between Nov. 9 and Nov. 16. Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo disclosed the largest stake among them, at $27.21 million. The bank held 712,319 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF, worth about $20.52 million, and it also opened a new position of 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF, worth about $6.7 million.

UBS and Morgan Stanley disclosed XRP fund holdings of $1.91 million and $116,000, respectively. Most of the UBS position was in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF, and Morgan Stanley held funds from Franklin, REX-Osprey and Bitwise.

Sources indicate that JPMorgan Chase held 539 shares of the Bitwise fund, worth about $9,000, and National Bank of Canada held 330 shares of the same fund, worth about $5,500. Bank of Montreal held REX-Osprey and ProShares Ultra XRP shares worth $4,300.

In a recent development, the crypto portfolio of Goldman Sachs grew to $2.64 billion by the end of September, according to its 13F filing. The bank held about $1.28 billion in Bitcoin ETFs, and BlackRock's IBIT and Fidelity's FBTC accounted for $778 million and $398 million of that amount, respectively. Goldman also held about $1.22 billion in Ether funds, and BlackRock's ETHA accounted for $603 million of that amount.

Recent findings suggest that goldman held $144 million in XRP ETFs at the end of the third quarter, up from $87 million at the end of the second quarter. The bank's 13F filing for the first quarter indicated no XRP or Solana ETF holdings, and Goldman still held no Solana funds at the end of September.

The bank held shares of five spot XRP funds from Franklin Templeton, Bitwise, Canary, Grayscale and 21Shares, and its Franklin Templeton position was worth almost $48 million.

Besides, trading firm Jane Street reported $23.5 million in XRP funds, and Simplex Trading disclosed a $14 million stake in the Grayscale fund. EP Wealth Advisors raised its Volatility Shares XRP ETF holding by 37% to 18,400 shares, worth about $148,000.

A 13F filing only indicates long positions as of Sept. 30. It doesn't show whether the banks hedge those holdings with shorts, or what they did with the shares in October and November. Since then, XRP has fallen below $1, and on Tuesday morning, XRP was trading at $0.966.

#88039. Tech investor Bill Gurley says workers who went through the ‘college conveyor belt’ and chased safe jobs are at high risk of AI automation

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (757 w)
📖 Baca

Tech investor Bill Gurley says workers who went through the ‘college conveyor belt’ and chased safe jobs are at high risk of AI automation

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, professionals have taught for generations that succeeding in school and attending an elite university would guarantee a rewarding six-figure career.
  • Now, venture capitalist Bill Gurley cautions workers against blindly following the career blueprint.
  • “This is latest and fast, and it’s attacking jobs that haven’t been attacked in the past,” Gurley remarked during the On with Kara Swisher podcast earlier this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, professionals have taught for generations that succeeding in school and attending an elite university would guarantee a rewarding six-figure career. But within a matter of years, AI has disrupted the world of work, and it’s quickly taking over the office roles humans were once promised.

Now, venture capitalist Bill Gurley cautions workers against blindly following the career blueprint.

“This is latest and fast, and it’s attacking jobs that haven’t been attacked in the past,” Gurley remarked during the On with Kara Swisher podcast earlier this year. “It’s creating a lot of anxiety, but I don’t know that we can put it back in the bottle.”.

The prolific tech financier, famous for his early investments in Uber and Zillow, is skeptical the government could pass AI regulation or pull off a massive reskilling effort. So as the technology continues to automate traditionally stable and lucrative roles, like lawyers and software engineers, it’s imperative workers actually be invested in their profession—or risk facing the chopping block.

It has been revealed that “The people that are most at risk are the ones that are sitting idly in the job and don’t really have a why or a purpose for it,” Gurley stated. “A lot of the people that go through that college conveyor belt, that are chasing a safe job, that end up working as a widget or a cog in an industry they may not love—I think they are ripe for disruption.”.

The Benchmark Capital general partner acknowledges it’s easier noted than done, but the best blueprint is to “craft your own career path” and tailor it to an individual’s distinct skills.

For those who can’t switch sectors or become self-employed, AI can act as career “jet fuel” that can make them even better at their jobs and indispensable to their employers.

According to recent reports, “If it’s out of your control, I just would say understand what it’s capable of in your industry and be the most AI-aware person in your job,” Gurley advised. “You’re going to then be the last person that they want to get rid of.”.

It has been revealed that gurley explores the idea that chasing a career of passion is a strategic edge, and not fluffy advice, in his newest book Runnin’ Down a Dream. He’s also one of several business leaders questioning the efficacy of how young professionals are trained to approach college.

Sources indicate that the investor has noticed a few worrying trends that may inhibit young professionals from following their true aspirations, hurting their career success. Gurley explained that kids today are “programmed from a time perspective” more than other generations. The budding talent start worrying about having a stacked résumé from a young age, and now some colleges require students to apply with a major in mind.

Industry observers note that these restraints don’t allow them to freely explore what jobs they’d enjoy, instead funneling them into a professional path very rapidly. He believes that’s part of the reason why so many people are checked out at work—a group that’s most susceptible to disruption.

Sources indicate that “There seems to me to be somewhat of a problem out there in that people aren’t landing where they’re passionate about what they’re doing,” Gurley stated. “I don’t think it’s anyone’s fault, but I think we’ve turned the college matriculation process into this pressure cooker.”.

Former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky echoes some of Gurley’s philosophy about career success in the AI era. Workers won’t be able to simply coast on a glitzy Ivy League degree: They need to have passion for their professions and the necessary tech skills to succeed in their careers.

“My guess is that the future of work belongs not anymore to the people that have the fanciest degrees or went to the best colleges,” Roslansky noted during a fireside chat at the platform’s San Francisco office last year.

Instead, he predicted talent most likely to land a job and succeed are “the people who are adaptable, forward thinking, ready to learn, and ready to embrace these tools…It really kind of opens up the playing field in a way that I think we’ve never seen before.”.

Fei-Fei Li, a Stanford professor and CEO of AI startup World Labs, dubbed the “Godmother of AI,” states being tech-savvy on the job matters more than anything else.

Now it’s essential for professionals to “superpower” themselves quickly with the tools, she advised.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on March 3, 2026.

#88037. Bitcoin's $90,000 Comeback Now Unlikely, Novogratz Warns

Bitcoin's $90,000 Comeback Now Unlikely, Novogratz Warns

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (437 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz noted that the odds of Bitcoin hitting $90,000 by the end of 2026 are slim in light of prevailing macroeconomic headwinds and the growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates.
  • During a live event with Anthony Scaramucci at the Digital Assets Forum in New York City, Novogratz was asked if Bitcoin could get back to $90,000 by the end of this year.
  • You need something to happen," Novogratz noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz noted that the odds of Bitcoin hitting $90,000 by the end of 2026 are slim in light of prevailing macroeconomic headwinds and the growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates.

During a live event with Anthony Scaramucci at the Digital Assets Forum in New York City, Novogratz was asked if Bitcoin could get back to $90,000 by the end of this year.

"Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," Novogratz noted.

His gloomy outlook comes as Bitcoin has struggled to rebound after a devastating drop that saw its price dip as low as $62,000 over the weekend. Bitcoin's price stood at around $64,600 on Nov. 17. The largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has declined for six consecutive weeks.

A shift in the U.S. monetary policy outlook, namely the prospect of more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, has been largely to blame for Bitcoin's decline, according to Novogratz.

"At the start of the year, everybody thought the Fed was going to be cutting now," he stated.

But high inflation and ongoing supply shocks have forced investors to readjust their expectations.

Sources indicate that "Inflation's going up. We've got inflation going up," Novogratz mentioned, warning that inflationary pressures could become increasingly entrenched.

"The Fed's going to hike. At least two more, probably three more," he said.

Novogratz predicted that the Fed would raise rates by 25 basis points in December and then hike again at its next meeting.

It has been revealed that he mentioned that higher rates, at least in the near term, tend to weigh on Bitcoin. But the higher cost of government borrowing could eventually provide support for the cryptocurrency.

"Yeah, later," he stated in response to the suggestion that higher borrowing costs could be a tailwind for Bitcoin.

Industry observers note that "First, you're gonna hike rates. Oh, sell gold, right? You're going to go to the dollar. It's so ingrained in peoples' heads," he said.

Industry observers note that "Carry costs going up," he said. Bitcoin doesn't offer the same yield as interest-bearing dollar assets.

"You don't make any interest on Bitcoin in dollars," he remarked.

In particular, Novogratz said that the massive rise in Treasury yields has been particularly detrimental to the crypto market.

In a recent development, "Literally 40 basis points in like four days of trading. So that's why crypto's down," he remarked.

He also stated that the massive crypto hack could still be weighing on investors' minds, adding to market jitters.

"I think in the back of their minds is the hack," he noted.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, promptly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads.
  • Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift.
  • “We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 13:28 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

Sources indicate that AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, promptly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

“We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”.

In a recent development, mcCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.).

Positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company prepares to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

Recent findings suggest that “Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill noted. “We went with commodity memory.”.

That choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap power without heavy regulatory hurdles. For inference providers monetizing new capacity, deployment speed is a big part of the appeal, according to McCaskill.

According to recent reports, “One of the groups of companies that we’re seeing a rise in right now and coming to us for product is these modular data centers, where they have a half megawatt or, 1 megawatt or 2.5 megawatt modular data center, and those can be deployed very quickly,” McCaskill remarked. “And the goal of a lot of these inference players is I want to get from land and power to monetizable tokens within 90 to 120 days. And those modular data centers, coupled with our technology, can be a great solution.”.

‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting upcoming software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting upcoming software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” mentioned Joe Duffy, the manufacturer’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how substantial we’re willing to dream.”.

In a recent development, the ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy stated there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The tech giant isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the firm in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The fresh products take that approach further:.

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

According to recent reports, both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise prepares.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy mentioned.

It has been revealed that AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy stated many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The fresh products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

In a recent development, plenty of manufacturer: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He remarked Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The fresh products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he stated.

Sources indicate that “This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Industry observers note that bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Sources indicate that neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy stated no launch in the manufacturer’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy remarked Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the manufacturer, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

It has been revealed that about 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building newly introduced products.

Sources indicate that despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy mentioned Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Sources indicate that asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy noted Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

#88034. Goodwill CEO says hiring managers are going behind their bosses’ backs and looking for workers with college degrees, not skills

Goodwill CEO says hiring managers are going behind their bosses’ backs and looking for workers with college degrees, not skills

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, more bad news for job seekers—especially non-grad Gen Zers.
  • It has been revealed that when major employers like Google, Microsoft, IBM, and Apple all eliminated their long-held degree requirements for jobs, other firms rushed to follow their example.
  • It has been revealed that goodwill’s CEO Steve Preston told Fortune that while most CEOs have good intentions, they can’t control every interview or job offer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, more bad news for job seekers—especially non-grad Gen Zers. Just because an employer claims it’s ditching degree requirements to recruit more diverse talent, that doesn’t mean its hiring managers are actually doing it.

It has been revealed that when major employers like Google, Microsoft, IBM, and Apple all eliminated their long-held degree requirements for jobs, other firms rushed to follow their example. But that promise may be limited to their job ads.

It has been revealed that goodwill’s CEO Steve Preston told Fortune that while most CEOs have good intentions, they can’t control every interview or job offer. And so the promise of skills-first hiring may not be reaching the millions of jobless Gen Zers who need it.

“Right now, employers are consistently saying they want to hire for skills, not necessarily degrees,” Preston stated. “But the proof is in the pudding. Not everybody does it.”.

He added: “What I hear from a lot of people is, ‘Yeah, the top says we need to do this,’ but when it gets to the hiring professionals, it doesn’t always trickle down.”.

The charity has more than 650 job centers and saw nearly 2 million people use its employment services last year, and Preston said he’s preparing for an influx of jobless Gen Zers thanks to automation.

While the opportunities for young people without degrees are certainly growing, Preston notes they’re ultimately still more likely to face unemployment than Gen Zers with a degree.

“What I’m seeing is, of the overall unemployment, people without college degrees have no jobs,” the 66-year-old CEO, who formerly served as the 14th United States secretary of housing and urban development, revealed. Research has shown that the matter is even more acute for young men.

“It’s much harder to find a job,” Preston added. “It’s really hitting college students right now in the marketplace. It’s really hitting young adults without college degrees.”.

So why are hiring managers still shutting the door on people who didn’t go down the higher education path, despite such a clear push to do the opposite?

“I think when somebody comes out with a four-year degree from college, there’s a certain sense that that person has a foundation that will be valuable in the workplace, and there’s a suspicion that if somebody hasn’t done that, they may be lacking some core skills,” Preston remarked, while pointing to critical thinking, team building, and communications as potential skills built from school projects and essays.

“So somebody with a strong collegiate background provides a high degree of comfort that these other capabilities are in place,” he added.

According to recent reports, “It’s also just easy to interview people who are like you, if you went to college, if you’ve gone down a particular pathway, you speak the same language, you have many of the same experiences. It’s much easier to connect with somebody who’s like you.”.

According to recent reports, for young people without degrees, Preston argued the key is proving you’ve built those prized skills elsewhere—whether that’s through upskilling, volunteering, or work experience. Even joining a sports team can help open doors because it teaches you confidence, teamwork, discipline, and more.

“Employers have to be able to see that many of those capabilities are acquired in different ways,” he said.

For closed-minded employers, Preston stressed the research is clear: Inclusive hiring isn’t just the right thing to do, it’s also good for business.

Sources indicate that “Organizations that have a much broader aperture in looking for talent are more likely to have the roles in their organizations filled; they’re much less likely to say that they’ve got deficiencies in their team; they’re more likely to say they’ve got a healthy workplace; and they often find higher engagement scores among their teams because of the culture that they’ve created,” he added. “Honestly, I think that’s important for society as well, on many levels.”.

A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on September 26, 2025.

According to Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson, there is plenty more to come for Cardano, as the blockchain's privacy-preserving sister chain, Midnight, reaches a huge milestone as its ecosystem continues to expand.

Charles Hoskinson made sure to clear up misunderstandings about whether he thought the work on Cardano was done.

"I never once mentioned Cardano is finished," Hoskinson said in a Nov. 15 post on X.

The comments came after he talked about the completion of Cardano's original roadmap, which raised some questions about his role in the blockchain's future.

He also called out the CEO of the Cardano Foundation, Frederik Gregaard, for not mentioning the Midnight chain when discussing everything the network has accomplished.

In his latest video, uploaded on Nov. 17, Hoskinson celebrated the fact that Midnight had just brought on board its first UK-based banking partner, Monument Bank.

Monument Bank is the first UK bank to offer interest-bearing tokenized retail deposits on a public blockchain, according to an announcement from the Midnight Foundation.

Up to £250 million in customer deposits will be added to Midnight in the first phase, and each tokenized deposit will be backed 1:1 by sterling cash held at the bank.

Monument Bank customers can now earn a fixed 5.2% annual equivalent rate on deposits for 12 months, all without having to deal with cryptocurrencies directly.

Hoskinson was very excited about the scale of the initiative, comparing the planned amount of deposits with the current decentralized finance ecosystem on Cardano.

"It's five times the TVL of Cardano," he said.

The £250 million is the planned initial size of the banking product, not a verified figure for how much is presently deposited on Midnight.

Hoskinson called this one of the most vital milestones in his career.

"This is just one of the many things to come, but I think it's one of the most significant things of at least my career," he remarked.

He added that the team behind Midnight had moved the originally scheduled hard fork from December to November to accommodate the technical needs of Monument Bank.

Despite the milestone, Hoskinson emphasized that it's only the first step in a much larger mission: bringing traditional financial assets onto Midnight.

According to recent reports, "This mission is not done if these assets are just strictly staying on Midnight. Needs to be expanded to Web3. But inherit from Midnight in terms of safety, security, privacy, simplicity," he noted.

Hoskinson thinks the main barrier to cryptocurrency adoption is the lack of trust among consumers. He believes that simplifying the user experience without compromising regulatory requirements will allow billions of people to join the blockchain economy.

Recent findings suggest that hoskinson also shared that there's a significant event coming up for the Midnight Foundation on Dec. 15. Developers will showcase future products and technological advancements scheduled for 2027.

#88031. Tech Report: Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1190 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale.
  • It has been revealed that healthcare is the clearest example.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

It has been revealed that healthcare is the clearest example. A firm can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

Industry observers note that the same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

Sources indicate that companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other. Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an key regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

Recent findings suggest that as an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health plans and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off. This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

Sources indicate that early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction. A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

Founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Recent findings suggest that has the founder or company addressed these challenges in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

It has been revealed that these challenges make the earliest stages of firm formation particularly important. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

At Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the tech giant is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

Recent findings suggest that that means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

Industry observers note that AI and newly introduced distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

In a recent development, the traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

In a recent development, moving quickly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

According to recent reports, for investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a organization needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

The most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A firm can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

Recent findings suggest that the same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59% to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss and its longest losing streak since February 2020.
  • Industry observers note that snider’s note mentioned the sell-off “expanded this week from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade,” noting that the S&P 500 excluding AI had held up until this week and is now 6% below its high.
  • Recent findings suggest that goldman’s note was written before Friday’s rout was fully in its data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59% to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss and its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% and is now down more than 2% for the year. Goldman Sachs notes the index is 12% below its Oct. 6 record, and its strategists have named the three things they’d need to see before calling a bottom.

Industry observers note that snider’s note mentioned the sell-off “expanded this week from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade,” noting that the S&P 500 excluding AI had held up until this week and is now 6% below its high. Goldman’s AI stock basket is down 32% since Oct. 6. Cyclical stocks have lagged defensives by 5 percentage points over the past 10 days.

Recent findings suggest that goldman’s note was written before Friday’s rout was fully in its data. Its exhibits are priced as of Nov. 19 and its hedge fund data run through that date. So the question is whether Friday supplied what the note was looking for — the situation could be even worse in markets than it acknowledged.

Goldman mentioned any one of the following would support a bottom and a recovery: news that raises confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a major drop in investor positioning.

Sources indicate that condition 1: AI earnings. This is the one the market is trying to test. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both, noting their combined sequential revenue growth fell from 75% in the second quarter to 48% in the third, while combined losses rose from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion. Reuters cited a valuation of about 40 times trailing sales for Anthropic. A US Bank Asset Management executive stated the valuation “assumes years of rapid growth.” Goldman’s own outlook says the AI outlook for 2028 and beyond “is highly uncertain.”.

Industry observers note that condition 2: the Fed. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, and the Fed meets Dec. 9. Goldman’s economists expect hikes in December and March, sending the federal funds rate to a peak of 4.25% to 4.5%. A dovish signal looks unlikely soon. Treasuries did rally sharply Friday as investors looked for safety, which is not the same as a Fed pivot. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday that the Fed will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%.

Condition 3: A big drop in investor positioning. This has often marked the end of past drawdowns.

Industry observers note that the first condition is unsettled, to say the least. Anthropic’s historic IPO turned into a sort of referendum on the entire AI trade, an unfair weight to put on a single, albeit remarkably important, organization. The company raised $93.5 billion after underwriters exercised an option, passing SpaceX’s $85.7 billion as the biggest IPO on record. The shares jumped 17% on Thursday, then gave most of it back Friday to close at $88.91, not far above the $83 IPO price. “Anthropic faded relatively quickly,” said Dakota Wealth’s Robert Pavlik. “I don’t think investors believe there’s something inherently wrong with the company… I think they’re just skeptical of this market.” Morgan Stanley, the underwriter tasked with stabilizing the shares, closed its support position, removing a potential pillar of support.

In a recent development, UBS noted the debate had shifted from whether AI investment will continue to whether it can generate enough revenue and returns for shareholders. A Capital Economics economist wrote that the IPO’s success while other AI stocks fell reveals the parts of the AI ecosystem “no longer move as one,” as chipmakers Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and AMD fell roughly 12% to 14%.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s 14% fall on Friday was its worst day in almost two years. It lost 22.9% on the week and is down 47.5% since Oct. 6, a loss of $2.7 trillion in market value. Reuters reported the SEC is probing its accounting practices. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. The VIX, Wall Street’s “Fear Gauge,” closed at 35.89, its highest in 19 months.

“It’s a meltdown right now,” remarked Arun Sundaram of CFRA Research. JPMorgan Asset Management’s David Kelly took the other view: “This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu.”.

Industry observers note that on the third condition, Goldman’s note says hedge funds have already cut back. Their net leverage is the lowest since April 2025. A companion report, Snider’s Hedge Fund Trend Monitor, says the most popular hedge fund longs were crowded into the AI trade and have lagged the S&P 500 by 14 percentage points over six months. That is among the worst stretches in the basket’s 20-year history. The note described the situation for hedge funds as “bruised and broadening.”.

But Goldman’s broader Sentiment Indicator is still above average. U.S. equity mutual funds and ETFs have taken in nearly $170 billion in the fourth quarter so far. Asset managers’ net equity futures positions are in the 82nd percentile of the past 10 years. Goldman’s equity strategists estimate the AI boom has lifted S&P 500 earnings 25% above trend. Goldman Research states AI capital spending produced “about half” of this year’s earnings growth.

The Street is split on whether this is the top. Capital Economics expects further declines. Goldman’s Nov. 17 outlook, written before the drop, forecast 8,700 by the end of 2027. In the Nov. 20 note, its range runs from about 5,800 to 8,100 depending on whether investors regain confidence in earnings. From Friday’s close, that is roughly 16% downside and 17% upside. Those percentages are my math, not Goldman’s.

After the 22 S&P 500 corrections since 1980, the index averaged a 4% return over the next three months. It rose in 17 of them. E*Trade’s research is less reassuring. Of the 14 times since 1983, the index first closed 10% or more below a record, five became bear markets.

Recent findings suggest that XRP is close to a $61 billion market cap, but its $0.9763 price still needs a real catalyst to recover. Dogecoin is extremely oversold after a 30% breakdown, with indicators hinting at a bounce. Solana is approaching $43 billion in market cap, yet it is stuck in the $70-$75 range at $73.75.

In a recent development, XRP's market capitalization is on the verge of breaking the $60 billion barrier after the massive drop. According to some aggregators, the price has already crossed the mark, while CoinMarketCap still reveals $61 billion.

The state of the market is very far from bullish: there's a good chance we won't see a proper, full-blown recovery sooner than next year, especially after the $6.1 billion wipeout on the cryptocurrency market.

However, XRP has multiple foundational advantages over competitors, such as stronger institutional backing and the use of its network for overseas transactions.

XRP is trading at $0.9763 after dipping to around $0.89 during the drop, and it is below $1 for the first time since mid-August. RSI touched the oversold zone near 30 and has bounced slightly since. The nearest moving average sits around $1.13, while the longest one is above $1.30.

Recent findings suggest that the asset has reached the area of the previous recovery, which will most likely push the market to the limit, as most traders want to break even on their positions rather than keep losing money. A potentially better time to buy XRP could be tied to the overall market recovery, hence the occurrence of a better market catalyst, which doesn't exist at this point.

The confirmation of a market recovery would only come if we witness specific signs of a bull run on larger-cap altcoins: higher highs and constant inflows into institutional products like ETFs.

Dogecoin lost more than 30% of its value in the breakdown that started on October 8. It destroyed all the gains Dogecoin had made in the past: September's peak is gone, and the price dropped to the lowest level in 4 years. However, it's not all doom and gloom.

DOGE is trading at $0.05963, which is around 43% lower than the September peak near $0.105. Dogecoin has been slowly tumbling for weeks, showing a continuous bearish dynamic, and it is now below all the moving averages. Volume spiked during the drop and has faded over the last two days.

According to multiple long-term momentum indicators, Dogecoin is extremely oversold. RSI and MVRV both suggest a bounce coming in the foreseeable future. While it's not guaranteed, obviously, there is potential. Most altcoins didn't see any spikes in selling because they were already oversold. The $0.068 area, where Dogecoin held in July and August, is already lost.

The cryptocurrency market moves in cycles, and the recent risk-on cycle in the global economy was exclusive to AI and tech stocks. The crypto market, on the other hand, missed out on it, and with no substantial gains and increased pressure in November, we got the double hit that destroyed hopes for a quick recovery.

Crypto might benefit from a transitional period on the market, even though it's not guaranteed by any means, as both risk tolerance and available funds are running dry.

Sources indicate that solana has almost reached the threshold of $43 billion market capitalization, according to data from CoinMarketCap. The asset is slowly moving back into the bullish zone after it joined other altcoins in a massive price drop. That's around 70% of XRP's $61 billion.

Solana mostly followed the general uptrend but tumbled swiftly due to the general reversal of the cryptocurrency market. SOL is trading at $73.75, down around 41% from the late September peak near $125. It dipped to approximately $67.5 during the drop and has bounced for two days, with RSI turning up from the oversold zone.

Every moving average on the chart sits above the price, with the nearest one around $87. Investors aren't buying en masse, but there is some accumulation, which could be tied to automated market making.

The correction on Solana is no different from other assets, and, unfortunately, SOL didn't show any additional resilience on the market.

From a price development perspective, the only positive outcome we are witnessing is the bounce from the August low zone, which might become support at some point, though that is not happening yet.

The dip below $70, which was the point of reversal back in August, is where some buy orders might be concentrated.

Currently, Solana is stuck in the approximately $70-$75 price range, and it seems unlikely to break out until it gets back to the moving averages at around $94-$96.

Industry News: Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, claims Stuttgart AI factory chief

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that in Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:48 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

Recent findings suggest that A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

Sources indicate that in Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

“It’s very notable to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller mentioned. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”.

It has been revealed that koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.).

Industrial users no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

“The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller said. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”.

It has been revealed that that pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

Industry observers note that “We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller remarked. “We have to look for the data.”.

Efficiency is part of the equation, too. The new system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

According to recent reports, “We learn more how the users are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller noted. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”.

#88024. Breaking: Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1254 w)

Breaking: Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten.
  • Sources indicate that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he mentioned, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

Sources indicate that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

Sources indicate that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

Recent findings suggest that I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your prepares for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is crucial. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in latest customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

In a recent development, before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying newly introduced things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Recent findings suggest that take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

Sources indicate that so figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a significant deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

I love setting goals. I’m a major believer in having a vision and building a proposal to get there. I’ve also learned that a latest calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

You don’t have to overhaul the whole firm all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

According to recent reports, there’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

Industry observers note that A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

According to recent reports, I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a firm.

According to recent reports, we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

Industry News: Only 18% of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills. A Wharton professor claims using AI is riskier for them

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The generation with the longest careers ahead of them appears to be the least interested in sharpening their AI skills, according to research from talent services firm Seramount released Thursday: Only 18% of Gen Z employees want to develop or improve their AI skills, compared with 36% of millennials, 46% of Gen Xers, and 43% of baby boomers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The generation with the longest careers ahead of them appears to be the least interested in sharpening their AI skills, according to research from talent services firm Seramount released Thursday: Only 18% of Gen Z employees want to develop or improve their AI skills, compared with 36% of millennials, 46% of Gen Xers, and 43% of baby boomers.

For younger workers, using AI could come with a different set of professional risks than it does for their more experienced colleagues.

“Because younger workers haven’t had the same amount of time in their career fields to build up their standing as experts, using a technology that blurs their own contribution to their work can feel especially risky,” Jessica Reif, an assistant professor of management at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, told Fortune.

The survey of more than 1,800 U.S. white-collar employees at companies with at least 500 workers, conducted in June through NORC’s AmeriSpeak panel, found that 58% of Gen Z employees use AI in their current roles, compared with 60% of baby boomers, 63% of millennials, and 67% of Gen Xers. Seramount defined Gen Z as workers 29 and younger.

In a recent development, that leaves a puzzle. Gen Z workers, often cast as digital natives, use AI at nearly the same rate as baby boomers but show far less interest in getting better at it.

Younger workers are considerably more concerned about what using AI might say about their own abilities.

According to recent reports, some 22% of Gen Z employees surveyed by Seramount worry that using AI could lead others to question their skills, compared with 10% of millennials and Gen Xers and just 8% of baby boomers. Only 27% of Gen Z employees feel comfortable acknowledging their use of AI for a work task, compared with between 47% and 53% of their older colleagues.

Those concerns are not entirely unfounded. In four experiments involving more than 4,400 participants, Reif, then at Duke University, and her co-authors Richard Larrick and Jack Soll found in a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that employees described as receiving help from AI were perceived as less competent, less diligent, and lazier than those described as receiving other forms of help or whose use of help wasn’t specified.

Industry observers note that the stigma could also influence hiring decisions. In one experiment, managers who used AI less frequently themselves favored candidates who did not use AI, while managers who were more frequent AI people favored candidates who used it daily.

The penalty in those experiments held regardless of the age of the employee being evaluated. But Reif remarked its consequences could be more substantial for workers who are still trying to establish themselves professionally.

“A senior employee who uses AI has a more substantial record of results that can offset doubts about their effort or ability, but an early-career employee doesn’t have that record yet so others might weight their AI use more heavily when evaluating them,” Reif mentioned.

Sources indicate that the pressure can work in the opposite direction, too. A survey of 3,001 professionals worldwide released Tuesday by the London School of Economics’ Inclusion Initiative and consulting firm Protiviti found that 48% of employees worry about being judged for not using AI enough at work, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it.

For workers at the beginning of their careers, that presents a dilemma: They need to demonstrate their ability to work with AI while also proving what they are capable of doing themselves.

Beyond concerns about their professional reputation, younger workers appear less convinced of the benefits of using AI in the first place.

Only 30% of Gen Z employees in Seramount’s survey believe AI helps them work more efficiently, compared with roughly half of their older colleagues. And 41% believe it improves the quality of their work, compared with 56% of Gen Xers.

Young people are also questioning whether the immediate benefits of AI could come at the expense of their long-term development. A survey by Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation, and GSV Ventures of 1,572 Americans aged 14 to 29, released in April, found that 80% believe using AI tools is very or somewhat likely to make learning more difficult for them in the future.

In a recent development, among employed Gen Z respondents, 48% believe the risks of AI in the workforce outweigh its benefits, compared with 15% who believe the opposite. Some 69% place greater trust in work completed without AI than in AI-assisted work.

That skepticism, as Fortune has reported, partly reflects how poorly schools, employers, and government have prepared young people for an AI economy.

Younger employees’ attitudes toward AI may also reflect the environments in which they are being asked to use it.

Only 27% of Gen Z respondents in Seramount’s survey stated their organization provides support to help them integrate AI into their work, compared with 38% of millennials and 43% of Gen Xers. Younger employees were also the least comfortable seeking help from colleagues on how to use AI tools, with only 18% saying they felt comfortable doing so, compared with 34% of baby boomers.

Seramount suggested that junior employees may also have less need for AI in their current roles or more limited access to enterprise AI tools.

The LSE and Protiviti research points to the importance of training in AI adoption across generations: 93% of employees who had received AI training used the technology at work, compared with 50% of those who had not.

Not all research suggests young workers are being left behind on training, though. The LSE and Protiviti study found that 66% of Gen Z employees had received AI training in the past year, compared with 40% of baby boomers. That study polled professionals worldwide, while Seramount surveyed only U.S. workers.

For employers, failing to engage their youngest employees in AI adoption could create a longer-term talent development problem, echoing warnings that automating entry-level roles could cost companies their future workforce.

“If Gen Z falls behind on AI, employers risk weakening their future leadership pipeline,” Diana Forster, senior director of research at Seramount, said in a press release. She called on employers to provide clearer guidelines, training, and opportunities for young employees to practice using the technology.

Despite the challenges young workers face in embracing AI, the technological disruption could also work in their favor.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes that periods of rapid technological change give people at the beginning of their careers a chance to gain a competitive advantage. As AI transforms how jobs are done and opens up new business opportunities, those with fresh ideas and new skills could have an edge over more established players.

“I think you want to start your career at a time of the greatest change, when the playing field is most open,” Altman said during an interview with Stanford’s Graduate School of Business in October, as previously reported by Fortune.

He added, “I think people with high potential, drive, ideas, a new way of looking at things, and new skills tend to do relatively well when the ground is shaking the most.”.

For workers concerned about being judged for using AI, Reif offered some advice.

“No matter their age, employees are increasingly in a position where they need to demonstrate their value above and beyond what AI can do,” Reif remarked. “Employees who are proactive in communicating how AI enables them to contribute more or in ways that would not have otherwise been possible may be able to counteract some of these perceptions.”.

Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

💡 Key Takeaways
